newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. African Zulu party out of constitution talks.
newsitem.headline: S. African Zulu party out of constitution talks.

text.p: Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi's Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) quit constitutional negotiations for a second time on Monday, dashing hopes of a South African consensus on a blueprint for post-apartheid rule.
IFP chief negotiator Walter Felgate told Reuters by telephone that Inkatha's National Council decided on Sunday not to participate further in the work of the Constitutional Assembly.
"It does not look as if there is any prospect of all-party agreement on a constitutional text, so there was no point in our continued participation," he said.

Inkatha quit the Constitutional Assembly (CA) in February last year, but returned last week after the Constitutional Court sent the draft text adopted in May back for further refinement on eight issues, including the authority of provincial and local overnments.
The decision to leave again after only six days torpedoed hopes of unanimity on what is likely to be the permanent structure of South Africa's post-apartheid society.

"The IFP seems to have decided to go against the tide of history in this country and I believe that history is going to judge them very harshly," Constitutional Assembly (CA) chairman Cyril Ramaphosa told Reuters.
He said the ANC would continue to meet Inkatha outside the framework of the CA, but said any hope of gradually remoulding the constitution through bilateral negotiations was "fool's comfort".
Political analysts said Inkatha's attitude was unfortunate but held no doomsday implications.

"You're going to continue to have a troublesome and querulous presence in KwaZulu-Natal province for as long as Inkatha rules the roost there, but it's not a particularly big or impressive roost," said political scientist David Welsh.
"However it also means a sizeable chunk of electoral support in the province remains uncommitted to the new structure."
KwaZulu-Natal province, which is ruled by Inkatha, has more than 21 percent of the country's people, but is poor and contributes less than 15 percent to gross national product.

The Constitutional Committee, comprising all the negotiators from the six political parties that have worked on the draft text, on Monday finalised amendments to address the Constitutional Court's criticisms.
"The job is done," Ramaphosa said after the committee approved accords presented by two specialist sub-committees.
"On Friday we adopt the constitution, which is a formality, and we send it back to the Constitutional Court," he said.
"I think we've done it...hopefully the Constitutional Court will agree to what we have decided here," chief National Party negotiator Roelf Meyer told Reuters.
Felgate said Inkatha would continue in separate talks with the ANC to press for constitutional recognition of the authority of tribal structures loyal mainly to Buthelezi.
"The role of the Amakhosi (chiefs) and traditional leaders is the burning issue of the moment. They have been stripped of all powers and this has to be addressed," he said.
The ANC, which won 62 percent of the vote in South Africa's first democratic elections in April, 1994, insists that all representatives must be elected.
ANC sources said Felgate approved a compromise offered by the party on Friday, but was unable to sell it to Buthelezi, who wants virtual autonomy for KwaZulu-Natal.
Inkatha won control of KwaZulu-Natal in the 1994 election, but took only 10 percent of the national vote and 48 of the 490 seats in the CA.
